summary: A description of MLTNET, a Telnet-like subsystem for TENEX written at BBN. It lets a user control several jobs on different ARPANET hosts from one console, switching between local command mode and remote mode. It was meant to help with debugging programs that use the network and is simpler than the TENEX user Telnet.

plainLanguage.summary: MLTNET lets a TENEX user manage connections to several ARPANET hosts from one console. The user selects a connection, types to that host, and can return to local commands to switch elsewhere.

subtitle: One TENEX console for controlling jobs on several hosts

tldr.problem: Users working with several remote hosts need a way to switch among their jobs from one console.
tldr.mechanism: MLTNET lets a user name connections, select one for direct interaction and buffer output from other connections.
tldr.outcome: The subsystem provides local command mode and remote mode for coordinating work across hosts.

today: RFC 339 describes MLTNET as a TENEX subsystem on BBN-TENEX. It explains how the program managed multiple remote connections from one console.

sections.title: A Multi-Host Console Tool
sections.content:
MLTNET is a TELNET-like subsystem for TENEX that lets a user control jobs running on different ARPANET hosts through one local console. The RFC says it is useful when work requires coordinated behavior across hosts, including debugging network programs.

MLTNET was installed as a subsystem on the BBN-TENEX host and was designed to be relatively simple and transparent during remote use.
sections.plainLanguage: One TENEX console can be used to work with jobs on different network hosts. This is useful when a task involves more than one host.

sections.title: Local and Remote Modes
sections.content:
In local mode, MLTNET accepts commands to associate a chosen name with a host, start a connection, list names or show network status. In remote mode, the console sends typed input to the selected host and displays its output. Output from other hosts is buffered while the user is in local mode or talking to another host.

When in remote mode, MLTNET passes control characters such as Control-C and Control-T to the remote site. In local mode those characters retain their usual TENEX effects.
sections.plainLanguage: Local mode accepts MLTNET commands. Remote mode sends your typing to one selected host, while output from other connections waits in a buffer.

sections.title: Commands and Remote Controls
sections.content:
Local commands include ASSIGN to name a connection, TALK to use it, NAMES to list known names, and FLUSH to close a connection. Other commands show host or network information, rename a connection, or leave MLTNET.

In remote mode, an exclamation mark introduces a MLTNET command for changing the current connection's settings. Typing two exclamation marks sends a literal exclamation mark to the remote host.
sections.plainLanguage: Commands such as ASSIGN and TALK name and select connections. In remote mode, type an exclamation mark before a control command, or type it twice to send one to the host.
